READING

**Step 1 – Net annual contribution from the Vantwyn operation**

| Item | Per season |
|---|---|
| Pollination fee: 400 × £168 | +£67,200 |
| Borage opportunity cost: 400 × £71 | −£28,400 |
| Colony replacement: 9% × 400 × £210 | −£7,560 |
| Haulage and labour | −£6,900 |
| **Net Vantwyn contribution** | **+£24,340** |

Over all three seasons: £24,340 × 3 = **£73,020**

**Step 2 – Equipment value under each course**

Under ORMSCLEUCH the pallets and lorry are sold to Ravensgate now for **£96,000**.

Under TREVANNOCK the contract runs to the end of the 2029 season, at which point the lorry's vale low emission zone permit has just expired (2030-01-01). Ravensgate's own estimate of its value after that is £20,000 as a farm vehicle. The pallets will be three seasons older; their residual is not stated, but worn 100-unit pallet stock is unlikely to recover the gap. I treat the terminal equipment value conservatively at £20,000–£25,000.

**Step 3 – Undiscounted comparison**

| | TREVANNOCK | ORMSCLEUCH |
|---|---|---|
| Incremental Vantwyn income | £73,020 | — |
| Equipment proceeds | ~£20,000–£25,000 | £96,000 |
| **Total** | **~£93,000–£98,000** | **£96,000** |

On a simple cash-sum basis the two are within a few thousand pounds of each other. At the optimistic end TREVANNOCK is fractionally ahead; at the central estimate they are essentially level.

**Step 4 – Time value**

The £96,000 arrives before 28 November 2026. The Vantwyn income arrives in three annual tranches across 2027–2029, and the kit residual arrives after 2030. Discounting at even a modest 5 % gives:

- PV of £24,340/year over three years starting 2027: ≈ £66,300
- PV of £20,000–£25,000 in ~3.5 years: ≈ £17,000–£21,000
- Total PV of TREVANNOCK incremental flows: ≈ **£83,000–£87,000**

Against £96,000 in hand now, ORMSCLEUCH leads by roughly **£9,000–£13,000** on a discounted basis, and the gap widens at any higher cost of capital.

**Step 5 – Risk loading on TREVANNOCK**

The 9 % spray-loss figure comes from what happened to Whinnerdale Bees on the same programme at the same kind of grower; Vantwyn will not alter that programme. The loss rate is therefore a floor, not a point estimate. Each additional percentage point of loss costs a further £840 per season (4 colonies × £210). If losses ran at 12 % rather than 9 % the annual net contribution would fall from £24,340 to £21,820, and the three-season total to £65,460 — narrowing the undiscounted case further and making the discounted case clearly negative against the £96,000 in hand.

**Step 6 – The Coldharbour and Nyefield upside**

These two vale growers have asked for a price for 2028. That is an enquiry, not a contract. The salient fact is that the three contracts that originally funded the migratory investment have all failed to renew. A second enquiry becoming a signed, paying contract cannot be assumed, and even if it did materialise the Vantwyn commitment already absorbs all 400 migratory colonies. Expansion would require raising and moving additional colonies, with associated costs and risks. The optionality exists but carries substantial execution and renewal risk given recent history.

**Step 7 – The queen rearing shed**

Ravensgate's offer does not include the shed. It remains on the books either way, but under ORMSCLEUCH it is no longer needed to produce 36 replacement colonies a season and may be repurposed or sold separately. This is an unquantified but real additional benefit of ORMSCLEUCH.

**Step 8 – Strategic coherence**

The migratory arm was built for three contracts, all of which lapsed. It has been idle for a full season. Keeping it alive for one new contract, at margins that barely justify the capital tied up, adds operational complexity and retains exposure to a spray programme that the grower will not modify. ORMSCLEUCH does not sacrifice the core business; it removes a loss-making satellite and restores a single, clean operation around 640 colonies and two proven honey lines.

**Step 9 – Verdict**

Financially, ORMSCLEUCH is ahead once time value is applied, and the lead increases under any realistic spray-loss scenario above 9 %. Strategically, selling into a known offer price (£96,000) before it closes is preferable to retaining kit that loses its permit value on a fixed date and whose eventual realisation is uncertain. The Coldharbour/Nyefield prospect is real but insufficient to reverse a conclusion that already holds on the primary numbers.

---

READING
The Vantwyn net contribution over three seasons (£73,020) is arithmetically close to the Ravensgate equipment offer (£96,000) on a simple-sum basis, but once time value is applied — the £96,000 arrives in late 2026 while the Vantwyn income is spread across 2027–2029 and the residual kit value falls to roughly £20,000 after the lorry's low emission zone permit expires — ORMSCLEUCH holds a discounted lead of the order of £9,000–£13,000 before any allowance for spray losses running above the already-damaging 9 % benchmark, the management overhead of a two-strand operation, or the pattern of pollination contracts failing to renew that gave rise to the choice in the first place.

CALL
  ORMSCLEUCH

GROUNDS
  The present value of the Ravensgate sale (£96,000 now) exceeds the discounted net Vantwyn income over three seasons plus the post-permit lorry residual, and that financial lead widens under any spray-loss rate above the 9 % already observed on the same programme.
